Ophthalmology · published research

Inclusion conjunctivitis

In infected guinea pigs, wIRA/VIS reduced clinical pathology scores and chlamydial load. A related safety report found no treatment-associated change in measured retinal or corneal stress markers.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

In infected guinea pigs, wIRA/VIS reduced clinical pathology scores and chlamydial load. A related safety report found no treatment-associated change in measured retinal or corneal stress markers.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact inclusion-conjunctivitis category contains one guinea-pig treatment publication. A related 2021 publication mapped from the same wIRA/VIS research program assesses heat- and stress-responsive proteins in guinea-pig ocular tissues. These are separate publications, and overlap in animal cohorts cannot be excluded from the source information. No human clinical study is listed. Inic-Kanada et al. 2020 Frohns et al. 2021

Human and clinical evidence

No treatment study in people with inclusion conjunctivitis was identified. The available outcomes concern laboratory infection and animal clinical signs, so they do not establish human symptom resolution, microbiological cure, visual benefit, or reduced transmission.

Animal evidence

In a guinea-pig model infected with Chlamydia caviae, water-filtered infrared A combined with visible light reduced clinical pathology scores at days 7 and 14 and lowered conjunctival chlamydial load at measured points through day 14 compared with infected, untreated controls. This is a disease-model result rather than evidence of efficacy against human trachoma or other causes of conjunctivitis.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

Related wIRA/VIS experiments in the broader research program report effects on chlamydial infectivity in cell systems. The 2021 guinea-pig ocular-tissue report found no detectable treatment-associated changes in selected heat- or stress-responsive proteins in retina and cornea 19 days after exposure. These findings are limited safety markers, not a comprehensive toxicology assessment.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The animal protocol used a 595–1400 nm range at 2100 W/m², comparing single and double exposures with sham treatment. This broad-band combination includes infrared and visible light, so effects cannot be attributed to one wavelength. Animal dose and exposure geometry do not define a human regimen.

Interpretation

The findings support further preclinical evaluation of wIRA/VIS against ocular chlamydial infection. They do not establish clinical efficacy or safety in people. A human study would need a defined comparator, infection measures, symptom outcomes, and a controlled exposure protocol.

Evidence strength in source summaryGuinea-pig infection and inflammation: Preclinical signal Human outcomes: No direct evidence
Publications and records1 direct animal publication (guinea-pig infection study).

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The direct evidence is one guinea-pig infection study reporting lower clinical inflammation and chlamydial load after wIRA/VIS exposure. A related tissue-safety publication examines stress markers, likely in a related model. No human clinical trial is listed, and the combination includes visible and infrared light.

Publication and study types

  • One related 2021 ocular-tissue safety publication is mapped from the same wIRA/VIS program and may overlap in experimental cohort.
  • The studies are not human clinical trials.
  • No unique animal cohort count can be established from the source records.

Research countries listed

  • Austria
